sec.title: Background
sec.p: Ovarian cancer remains a formidable therapeutic challenge due to late diagnosis, high recurrence rates, and limited treatment options. Mesothelin (MSLN) is highly expressed in ovarian cancer, making it a promising target for immunotherapy. Given this target profile, the authors developed a novel T‐cell receptor (TCR)‐like chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T‐cell therapy targeting MSLN, designated KT127.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A first‐in‐human, dose‐escalation trial of KT127 was conducted following preclinical evaluation in vitro and in vivo. A combination of rapid titration and a standard “3 + 3” dose‐escalation design was implemented. Eleven patients received KT127 at doses ranging from 1 × 106 to 2 × 107 cells/kg following lymphodepletion. The primary objectives were to assess the safety and tolerability of KT127. Secondary objectives included overall survival, disease control rate (DCR), and progression‐free survival as efficacy measures. Quality of life (QOL) was assessed using the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer QLQ‐OV28 questionnaire.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: No dose‐limiting toxicities, cytokine release syndrome, or immune effector cell‐associated neurotoxicity syndrome were observed. The DCR was 80% (95% confidence interval, 44.4%–97.5%). QOL assessments indicated improvement in abdominal/gastrointestinal symptoms post‐treatment (p = .037), with no significant deterioration in other domains. Proteomic analysis identified differential expression of kallikrein‐related peptidases (KLK13, KLK14) and chemokine CXCL17 at baseline, potentially linked to treatment outcomes.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This study highlights that KT127 has a manageable safety profile and shows preliminary biological activity in patients with advanced ovarian cancer, particularly those who have failed multiple lines of therapies.

abstract.p: A first‐in‐human study evaluated a mesothelin‐targeted T‐cell receptor‐like CAR T‐cell therapy in advanced ovarian cancer. The treatment showed manageable safety and preliminary disease control.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Ovarian cancer is the eighth most common cancer among women worldwide, both in terms of incidence and mortality. 1 High‐grade serous carcinoma is the most prevalent subtype. It is often diagnosed at an advanced stage due to the lack of screening methods and is characterized by high recurrence and mortality rates. 2 Current treatments, including surgery, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, improve survival but are limited by recurrence and drug resistance, 3 necessitating more effective strategies.

Recently, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T‐cell therapy has garnered attention for its potent antitumor activity, particularly in hematologic malignancies. However, its application in solid tumors, such as ovarian cancer, has faced significant hurdles. Challenges such as off‐target effects, antigen escape, tumor heterogeneity, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment limit its efficacy in these cancers. 4

Mesothelin (MSLN) is a cell‐surface glycoprotein present in the serum of tumor patients as a soluble related peptide (SMRP). 5 In normal tissues, MSLN expression is restricted to pleural, peritoneal, pericardial, and mesothelial cells. 4 However, MSLN is highly expressed in many malignant tumors and was initially identified in mesothelioma and ovarian cancer. It has been demonstrated as a promising target for antibody‐based therapies in murine systems. 6 , 7 Previous studies have shown that targeted MSLN immunotherapy has a favorable safety profile. 5 , 8 , 9 Although many early clinical trials of anti‐MSLN CAR T cells have been conducted over the past decade, 10 limited clinical trial data fully evaluate the safety and efficacy of these therapies, warranting further investigation.

In this context, we introduce a novel TCR‐like CAR T‐cell therapy (KT127) targeting MSLN. Unlike conventional second‐generation CARs, which are unable to generate the complete spectrum of T‐cell receptor (TCR) signals, KT127 integrates the strengths of both CAR T‐cell and TCR T‐cell therapies. This innovative design combines the antigen–antibody‐specific recognition ability of CAR T cells with the signaling regulatory characteristics of TCR, potentially overcoming the limitations of conventional CAR T‐cell therapies in solid tumors. The KT127 construct includes anti‐MSLN‐CD3e‐Bzip/CD4‐Azip elements, encoded by a bicistronic lentiviral vector and separated by an F2A linker. This unique design improves T‐cell migration and sustains long‐term functionality, resulting in more effective antitumor activity than conventional CAR T cells targeting the same antigen. We first demonstrated the strong antitumor effects and low systemic toxicity of KT127 through laboratory and animal studies (unpublished data from our laboratory). Based on these data, we then launched a clinical trial in patients with MSLN‐positive advanced ovarian cancer to evaluate its safety and effectiveness in real‐world settings.

sec.title: Preclinical methods
sec.p: Detailed descriptions of all preclinical experimental procedures, including cell culture, lentivirus preparation, flow cytometry, ELISA, cytotoxicity assays, and the in vivo xenograft model, are provided in Supporting Methods S3.

sec.title: Clinical trial design
sec.p: This single‐arm, open‐label, dose‐escalation study was conducted at Zhongda Hospital, Southeast University. The study protocol was authorized by the institutional review board (2023ZDSYLL115‐P01) and registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05963100). Written informed consent was obtained from all patients following the Declaration of Helsinki. All patients underwent lymphodepletion before CAR T‐cell transfusion and were required to undergo computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging at baseline and at 28 days after a single intravenous transfusion of KT127. The primary objectives were to evaluate the safety and tolerability of KT127. The primary study end points included maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and adverse events (AEs). The secondary study end points included overall survival (OS), disease control rate (DCR), and progression‐free survival (PFS).

A rapid titration combined with a standard “3 + 3” dose‐escalation design was employed. The starting dose was selected with reference to prior clinical studies of CAR T‐cell products, 11 , 12 in accordance with regulatory guidance for cell therapy products issued by the National Medical Products Administration. To minimize exposure to sub therapeutic doses, dose level 1 (DL1) enrolled only one patient. If this patient experienced a grade ≥2 AE related to the investigational product, the dose level would be expanded per the standard “3 + 3” design. Dose levels 2 through 4 followed the conventional “3 + 3” scheme and MTD will be determined. The corresponding CAR T‐cell doses for each level were as follows: DL1, 1 × 106 cells/kg; DL2, 3 × 106 cells/kg; DL3: 1 × 107 cells/kg; and DL4: 2 × 107 cells/kg.

All patients underwent lymphodepletion before CAR T‐cell infusion. The initial regimen included cyclophosphamide (250 mg/m2/day, days –4 to –2) and fludarabine (25 mg/m2/day, days –4 to –2). After the first three DL2 patients showed limited CAR T‐cell activation and expansion, the regimen was amended: cyclophosphamide (250 mg/m2/day, days –4 to –2), fludarabine (25 mg/m2/day, days –4 to –3), and albumin‐bound paclitaxel (100 mg, day –3). This adjustment was supported by preclinical and early clinical data showing that paclitaxel can remodel the tumor microenvironment, reduce immunosuppressive stromal and myeloid components via secreted protein acidic and rich in cysteine interactions, and improve immune‐cell trafficking. 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 Similar conditioning has been safely applied in other solid tumor CAR T‐cell studies, showing feasibility and improved CAR T‐cell expansion. 17 , 18 The amendment was approved by the institutional review board, and one additional patient was enrolled to confirm safety before dose escalation continued. All subsequent patients received the revised regimen.

Adverse events were assessed and categorized throughout the study period. Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell‐associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) were graded according to the ASTCT 2019 criteria, and the rest of the adverse events were graded according to the US Department of Health and Human Services Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events 5.0 criteria. A DLT was characterized by any of the following events assessed as related to KT127: any grade ≥4 hematologic toxicity persisting beyond specified durations; grade ≥3 thrombocytopenia with concurrent bleeding; grade ≥3 nonhematologic toxicity (except for specified exceptions); grade 3 CRS that did not resolve to grade ≤2 within 7 days or any grade 4 CRS; or any grade ≥3 ICANS. For comprehensive details, please refer to Supporting Methods S2. MTD was defined as the highest dose at which no more than two of at least six evaluable subjects experienced DLTs.

sec.title: Patient eligibility criteria
sec.p: Primary inclusion criteria were as follows: histopathologically confirmed platinum‐resistant advanced ovarian cancer, ≥26% immunohistochemistry (IHC) mesothelin positivity of the tumor tissue, age between 18 and 70 years, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0 to 1, and expected survival >3 months. Primary exclusion criteria included a history of other malignancies within 5 years, active infections, autoimmune diseases, and prior receipt of other cytogenetic products within 6 months. Detailed information is available in Supporting Methods S1.

sec.title: MSLN IHC testing and scoring
sec.p: Tumor MSLN expression was evaluated by immunohistochemistry on formalin‐fixed, paraffin‐embedded tissue sections (3–5 μm) mounted on positively charged slides. Mesothelin was detected using a validated antibody (Abcam #ab196235; RRID: AB_3665950) at 1:4000 dilution with the OptiView DAB IHC Detection Kit on a BenchMark GX platform.

Staining intensity was scored as 0 (<1% positive tumor cells), 1+ (1%–25% positive tumor cells), 2+ (26%–50% positive tumor cells), 3+ (51%–75% positive tumor cells), and 4+ (≥76% positive tumor cells). Tumor cells with intensity ≥2+ were defined as MSLN‐positive. The proportion of positive tumor cells was calculated as the number of membrane‐stained cells divided by total tumor cells. A cutoff of ≥26% was applied to define eligibility, consistent with prior clinical studies of MSLN‐targeted therapies. 19 , 20 , 21

sec.title: Peripheral blood cytokine assay
sec.p: Cytokines were measured in peripheral blood of patients collected at multiple time points using chemiluminescence and immunofluorescence techniques, specifically at baseline (pre‐infusion) and on days 1, 4, 7, 10, 14, 21, and 28 post‐infusion.

sec.title: Serum CA125 monitoring
sec.p: Patients' serum samples were collected to monitor CA125 levels dynamically at baseline and on days 14, 28, 56, and 84 post‐treatment.

sec.title: Life quality
sec.p: Patients' quality of life (QOL) was assessed using the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) QLQ‐OV28 questionnaire at baseline and at the first post‐infusion imaging assessment (day 28).

sec.title: Definition of efficacy endpoints
sec.p: The secondary study end points of this study were defined as follows: OS was defined as the time from the date of KT127 infusion to the date of death from any cause. Patients who were still alive at the time of data cutoff were censored at their last known alive date. PFS was defined as the time from the date of KT127 infusion to the date of first documented disease progression according to Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) 1.1 criteria or death from any cause, whichever occurred first. Patients without an event were censored at the date of their last tumor assessment. DCR was calculated as the proportion of patients who achieved a best overall response of complete response, partial response (PR), or stable disease (SD) based on RECIST 1.1 criteria.

sec.title: Graphs and statistical analysis
sec.p: NovoExpress software v1.6.0 was used for flow cytometry data analysis. GraphPad Prism 10.1.2, Rv4.3.2, and Microsoft Excel 2021 were used for other data analysis. Some images were created with BioRender. For the preclinical trials section, unless otherwise specified, all data represent at least three independent experiments and are expressed as mean ± SEM. Statistical significance between groups was evaluated using Student’s t‐test, with p ≤ .05 defined significant.

sec.title: Four novel CAR structures targeting MSLN
sec.p: We designed a novel TCR‐like CAR architecture based on the second‐generation CAR structure and the T‐cell antigen coupler. The TCR‐like CAR construct comprises the anti‐MSLN‐CD3e‐Bzip/CD4‐Azip elements, which are encoded by a bicistronic lentiviral vector separated by an F2A linker. Specifically, anti‐MSLN‐CD3e‐Bzip was engineered by fusing the anti‐mesothelin antibody SS1 to the human CD3e subunit and Bzip. Meanwhile, CD4‐Azip was created through the fusion of CD4 and Azip (Figure 1A). Azip and Bzip are two proteins capable of interacting with each other to form a leucine zipper structure. 22 When Azip and Bzip interact with each other, their leucine residues align in a zipper‐like fashion, enabling the formation of a stable dimer. By harnessing the signaling capabilities of the entire TCR and CD4 coreceptor in this manner, the TCR‐like CAR achieves enhanced T‐cell trafficking, long‐term functional persistence, and superior antitumor activity compared to traditional CAR T cells with the same specificity. Using a lentiviral gene delivery system, we constructed four novel CAR structures targeting MSLN: CD3e‐Bzip/SS1 scFv‐CD4‐Azip (SS1‐CD4/CD3e), SS1 scFv CD3e‐Bzip/CD4‐Azip (SS1‐CD3e/CD4), SS1 scFv‐CD4‐Azip (SS1‐CD4), and SS1 scFv CD3e‐Bzip (SS1‐CD3e) (Figure 1B). Flow cytometry was used to analyze SS1 scFv expression on the T‐cell surface across four different TCR‐like CAR designs and to quantify their CAR positivity rates. Among these, SS1‐CD3e CAR T cells exhibited the highest scFv expression level at 74.08% and the highest CAR positivity rate at 80.76%. SS1‐CD3e/CD4 CAR T cells (also known as KT127) demonstrated scFv expression and CAR positivity rates of 50.07% and 61.97%, respectively (Figure 1C,D). Relative F(ab')2 mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) analysis confirmed that SS1‐CD3e CAR T cells had the highest surface scFv expression, which was significantly greater than that of SS1‐CD4/CD3e CAR T cells and SS1‐CD4 CAR T cells (p = .0002), although not significantly different from KT127 (Figure 1E).

caption.p: Design and surface expression of TCR‐like CAR. (A) Schematic diagram of the lentiviral vector expressing TCR‐like CAR transgenes. CD3e, CD3ε TCR subunits; Bzip, leucine zipper; 2A, 2A peptide; SS1 scFv, anti‐MSLN single‐chain fragment variable; CD4, truncated CD4 coreceptor; Azip, leucine zipper. (B) The natural TCR complex in four TCR‐like CAR. (C) Representative flow cytometry profile of ss1 scFv on the surface of TCR‐like CAR T. (D) Representative flow cytometry profile of scFv on the surface of TCR‐like CAR T cells. (E) Surface relative F(ab′)2 MFI in primary human T cells. Data are presented as mean ± SEM from eight independent donors (n = 8). Statistical significance was determined by the Mann–Whitney test. CAR indicates chimeric antigen receptor; MFI, mean fluorescence intensity; MSLN, mesothelin; TCR, T cell receptor.

sec.title: Cytotoxicity of TCR‐like CAR T cells in vitro
sec.p: Before evaluating cytotoxicity in vitro, investigators confirmed high MSLN expression on the surface of the SKOV3‐MSLN cell line using flow cytometry (Figure S1A). Real‐time cellular analysis assays demonstrated that both SS1‐CD3e/CD4 CAR T cells and SS1‐CD3e CAR T cells exhibited significant, dose‐dependent antitumor activity (Figure S1B,C). Notably, SS1‐CD3e/CD4 CAR T cells showed the highest killing efficiency, with enhanced tumor‐killing effects at higher effector‐to‐target (E:T) ratios and longer coculture periods. In contrast, neither SS1‐CD4/CD3eCAR T cells nor SS1‐CD4 CAR T cells demonstrated significant antitumor activity, particularly at lower E:T ratios of 2.5:1 and 5:1.

To further assess CAR T‐cell functional activation, enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) was used to measure IFN‐γ secretion (Figure S1D). Consistent with the cytotoxicity results, SS1‐CD3e/CD4 CAR T cells produced significantly higher levels of IFN‐γ than other groups (p < .05), indicating stronger functional activity. These findings highlight the potent in vitro antitumor and functional activity of SS1‐CD3e/CD4 CAR T cells (KT127).

sec.title: Antitumor activity of TCR‐like CAR T cells in vivo
sec.p: We established a mouse ovarian cancer xenograft model using the SKOV3‐MSLN cell line. Given the limited in vitro antitumor activity of SS1‐CD4/CD3e CAR T cells and SS1‐CD4 CAR T cells, these groups were excluded from further in vivo experiments. Instead, traditional second‐generation CAR T cells (SS1‐BBζ CAR T) were included for comparison. On day 18 after subcutaneous tumor injection, mice were treated with SS1‐BBζ CAR T cells, SS1‐CD3e/CD4 CAR T cells, SS1‐CD3e CAR T cells, or mock CAR T cells (Figure S2A). Among the four groups, SS1‐CD3e/CD4 CAR T cells demonstrated the greatest tumor growth inhibition without causing significant changes in mice's body weight, indicating minimal systemic toxicity (Figure S2B–D).

sec.title: Clinical trial results
sec.p: A total of 11 patients were screened from August 7, 2023, to August 15, 2024. All patients signed informed consent forms, underwent leukapheresis, and completed CAR T‐cell transfusion. The flow of the clinical trial design is summarized in Figure 2A. A total of 10 patients were included in the final analysis after one patient voluntarily withdrew from the study due to disease progression. Of the 10 patients, one received a low dose (1 × 106 cells/kg), four received a medium dose (3 × 106 cells/kg), three received a medium‐high dose (1 × 107 cells/kg), and three received a high dose (2 × 107 cells/kg) of CAR T cells (Figure 2B). By the time of the first tumor imaging assessment (28 days post‐infusion), one patient withdrew because of rapid disease progression, thus a total of 10 patients were included in the final analysis.

caption.p: Study design and patient allocation. (A) Clinical trial design overview. Created with BioRender.com. (B) Study schema and patient distribution. The trial adopted an integrated rapid titration/“3 + 3” dose‐escalation design, enrolling a total of 11 patients (n = 11, 10 evaluable). The addition of a fourth patient in medium dose level was intended to preliminarily assess the safety of a revised regimen before proceeding to higher dose levels.

sec.p: The baseline characteristics of all patients are summarized in Table 1. The median age was 53.5 years (range: 45–69 years). Three patients (30%) had ascites and one (10%) had pleural effusions. All patients had advanced, recurrent, or refractory ovarian cancer with an ECOG performance status of 1. Pathologically, all 10 patients (100%) were diagnosed with high‐grade serous carcinoma. All patients had advanced, recurrent, or refractory ovarian cancer with a median of 4.5 prior lines of systemic therapy (range, 2–8), including chemotherapy (n = 10), radiotherapy (n = 1), immunotherapy (n = 3), and targeted therapy (n = 10). Overall, the patients included in this study had poor prognostic features and had undergone multiple lines of prior therapy.

fn.p: Abbreviations: CAR T, chimeric antigen receptor T; ECOG, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group; HGSOC, high‐grade serous ovarian cancer; MSLN, mesothelin; PD, progressive disease; SD, stable disease.

sec.title: Safety and adverse events
sec.p: KT127 demonstrated a favorable safety profile, with no cytokine release syndrome (CRS) or immune effector cell‐associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) observed. All 10 evaluable patients experienced at least one AE. Only one patient experienced one serious adverse event (SAE), but there was no treatment‐related death. The most commonly AEs were hematologic toxicity events, including anemia (2 of 10), leukopenia (6 of 10), neutropenia (4 of 10), lymphopenia (8 of 10), thrombocytopenia (3 of 10), and leukocytosis (2 of 10), of which ≥grade 3 events occupied 51.8%. Hematologic toxicity subsided to baseline within 21 days after infusion in the majority of patients and was primarily attributed to lymphocyte depletion during preconditioning. In addition, AEs related to gastrointestinal toxicity were also frequently observed, with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea being the most common symptoms. Most gastrointestinal issues were reversible, with only one case of grade ≥3 observed, where adhesive intestinal obstruction was observed on day 22 before infusion and persisted. This was likely related to the malignant tumor rather than the treatment. A detailed summary of the AEs experienced by all patients throughout the study was shown in Table 2.

Of all the AEs potentially related to the treatment of CAR T cells, the most noteworthy was that one patient in the median‐high dose level group, who tolerated the CAR T‐cell infusion without infusion‐related events and experienced no DLT events during the observation period, developed grade 4 platelet count reduction on day 96 post‐infusion, which was promptly reported as SAE by the investigator. The patient had a history of severe myelosuppression from prior chemotherapy, and subsequent pathogen testing revealed infections with Neo coronavirus, Epstein‐Barr virus, and chlamydia—all of which can contribute to platelet reductions. The investigators determined this SAE was likely unrelated to the CAR T‐cell infusion. No cases of CRS or ICANS were observed in any of the 10 patients, and no DLTs were reported. Consequently, the MTD could not be determined. Overall, these findings demonstrate the favorable safety and tolerability of KT127.

sec.title: Clinical activity
sec.p: The primary analysis was conducted with a data cutoff date of January 1, 2025. Based on the RECIST 1.1 criteria for evaluating clinical efficacy in solid tumors, of the 10 evaluable patients, eight (80%) patients achieved SD, whereas two (20%) patients experienced progressive disease (PD) as their best overall response, resulting in a DCR of 80%. Despite these responses, disease progression occurred in all 10 enrolled patients within a 9‐month observation period, with four individuals surviving until the last follow‐up. PFS was 84 days (95% CI, 28–not reached), and OS was 129 days (95% CI, 101–not reached) (Figure 3B,C).

caption.p: Evaluation of clinical responses and survival outcomes. (A) Tumor burden percentage changes were visualized using a waterfall plot representation. (B and C) PFS and OS of all evaluable patients were analyzed by the Kaplan–Meier method. The median PFS was 84 days (95% CI, 28–not reached). The median OS was 129 days (95% CI, 101–not reached). (D) Swimmer plot describing patient history from initial infusion through death or most recent follow‐up. OS indicates overall survival; PFS, progression‐free survival.

sec.p: Three patients showed a reduction in the sum of target lesion diameters (Figure 3A). Notably, patient 3, initially assessed as having stable disease at 6 months post‐infusion, showed a 50% reduction from baseline at 9 months (Figure 4). However, new hepatic lesions emerged, leading to PD classification. Another patient in the median dose level group exhibited a sustained reduction in posterior pancreatic lymph node lesions, with decreases of 37.5% at 1 month, 53% at 2 months, and 70% at 3 months post‐infusion, despite an overall increase in the total target lesion burden (Figure 4).

caption.p: Magnetic resonance imaging scan images of target lesions at baseline and during subsequent follow‐up assessments.

sec.p: In interpreting the disease control rate, it is important to note that two patients (patient 4 and patient 7) died during periods classified as stable disease. Patient 4 died of cancer‐related cachexia shortly after the last imaging confirming SD, whereas patient 7 died of a bowel obstruction. Additionally, patient 8 was taken off protocol due to refusal of continued imaging follow‐up.

Serum CA125 levels remained stable or declined following KT127 infusion, particularly at days 14 and 28, suggesting an early treatment effect (Figure S3F). These changes were generally consistent with radiographic assessments of tumor burden.

sec.title: Pharmacokinetics
sec.p: The expansion and persistence of TCR‐like CAR T cells were assessed using flow cytometry and real‐time quantitative PCR (qPCR) to measure CAR T‐cell counts and CAR gene copy numbers in peripheral blood. CAR gene copies in peripheral blood expanded rapidly after infusion, with a median peak at 7 days (range, 1–21 days), followed by a gradual decline over the next 28 days (Figure S3A). Notably, for patient 3, low levels of CAR T cells were detectable even 252 days after infusion, suggesting good long‐term persistence, which is also consistent with the continued shrinkage of the target lesion.

The data from flow cytometry and qPCR were consistent, showing a strong correlation between the peak amplification of CAR gene copies in peripheral blood and the number of infused TCR‐like CAR T cells (r = 0.8545, p = .0029) (Figure S3B). However, no correlation was found between the peak CAR gene copies or the number of infused TCR‐like CAR T cells and the best change in the sum of target lesion diameters (Figure S3D,E).

sec.title: Changes in peripheral blood cytokine levels
sec.p: Cytokine analysis of peripheral blood revealed significantly elevated levels of interleukin (IL)‐6 (Figure S3C), whereas other cytokines, including IL‐2, IL‐4, IL‐8, IL‐10, TNF‐α, and IFN‐γ, showed minimal changes. IL‐6 is known to activate downstream inflammatory signaling, either by binding to membrane receptors for classical signaling or to soluble receptors for transsignaling, thus playing an important role in the development of CRS. The marked increase in IL‐6 suggests that the activation and expansion of TCR‐like CAR T cells targeting MSLN triggered an inflammatory response. However, none of the patients developed CRS, indicating that the increase of IL‐6 was well controlled and did not lead to severe systemic toxicity. The modest changes in IL‐8 and IL‐10 levels may reflect localized immunomodulation rather than widespread activation. Additionally, the stable levels of IFN‐γ suggest that T‐cell activation remained controlled, which aligns with the soft activation strategy employed in this study and supports the favorable safety profile observed.

sec.title: Life quality assessment
sec.p: At baseline, the QOL for patients with advanced ovarian cancer was markedly impaired, both physically and in terms of self‐perception. In the EORTC QLQ‐OV28 abdominal/gastrointestinal symptoms domain, patients who received KT127 infusion showed improvement in symptoms compared to baseline at the time of their first imaging evaluation (p = .037) (Table 3). However, no significant changes were observed in the other six domains, including peripheral neuropathy, chemotherapy side effects, hormonal/menopausal symptoms, body image, attitude toward disease and treatment, and sexual function. Although the improvement in abdominal/gastrointestinal symptoms reached statistical significance, the mean change was less than 10 points—below the minimal important difference (MID) typically considered clinically meaningful. Therefore, this improvement should be interpreted as a mild symptomatic benefit rather than a clinically meaningful change. The relative contribution of CAR T cells in vivo effects versus the psychological impact on the patients remains uncertain.

sec.title: Comparison of plasma protein expression levels
sec.p: Plasma protein expression was analyzed in nine patients (Figure S4A). The nine patients were stratified into three groups based on the best overall response and duration of disease stability, with two patients having a best overall response of PD (PD group), three patients having a stable duration of disease of less than 3 months (SD_1 group), and four patients having a stable duration of disease of 3 months or more (SD_2 group). Plasma protein assays for these patients all passed quality control.

At baseline, kallikrein‐related peptidase 13 (KLK13) was significantly downregulated in the SD_1 group compared with the PD group (Figure S4B). The SD_2 group showed a significant upregulation of human kallikrein gene 14 (hK14, also known as KLK14) compared to the PD group (Figure S4C). Additionally, compared with the SD_1 group, the SD_2 group exhibited a significant downregulation of cornulin and a significant upregulation of C–X–C motif chemokine 17 (CXCL17) (Figure S4D).

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: Our study introduces a novel TCR‐like CAR T‐cell immunotherapy (KT127) that integrates the advantages of TCR T‐cell and CAR T‐cell therapies. The dissociation between elevated IL‐6 and the absence of CRS/ICANS highlights a key safety feature of our TCR‐like CAR. Its design, which harnesses the native CD3e/Lck signaling axis, promotes a self‐limiting T‐cell activation—sufficient for antitumor activity but restrained from progressing to a cytokine storm.

Regarding the efficacy of the clinical trial, KT127 demonstrated encouraging signs of disease control in a heavily pretreated, platinum‐resistant population. The median PFS of 84 days in our study is comparable to that historically reported for existing therapies in platinum‐resistant ovarian cancer, which typically demonstrate a median PFS of 3.0–4.0 months. 23 , 24 , 25 Although no objective responses were observed, the 80% disease control rate and the sustained tumor shrinkage in a subset of patients suggest that KT127 has biological activity. Future studies should focus on identifying predictive biomarkers and combination strategies to enhance the magnitude and duration of clinical benefit.

Regarding safety, KT127 was well tolerated in the 10 evaluable patients. No CRS or ICANS were observed, with only one SAE reported, which was deemed unrelated to the treatment. The absence of CRS and ICANS is particularly noteworthy, as these are common adverse reactions associated with conventional CAR T‐cell therapies, especially in solid tumors. 26 The favorable safety profile of KT127 may be attributed to its unique TCR‐like CAR structure, which enables soft activation of T cells, thereby reducing the risk of excessive cytokine production and systemic toxicity. QOL findings also support the tolerability of KT127. QOL findings indicated that KT127 treatment maintained overall patient well‐being, with observed improvements being less than the 10‐point MID. 27 , 28

The efficacy of TCR‐like CAR T cells may be influenced by several factors. First, tumor load plays a crucial role in determining efficacy. 29 High tumor burden not only increases the antigenic challenge for CAR T cells but also potentially impairs their effectiveness by triggering systemic inflammatory responses and immune dysregulation. 30 Second, there is heterogeneity in the degree of MSLN expression in patients, which is also an important factor affecting the efficacy of TCR‐like CAR T cells. For example, although the enrollment conditions of this study stipulated that the IHC MSLN positivity rate of the patient's tumor tissue was ≥26%, the evaluation criteria of MSLN expression and the enrollment requirements are currently not standardized internationally. Given that KT127 is an MSLN‐targeted therapy, a higher MSLN positivity rate likely increases the potential for therapeutic benefit. Third, the tumor microenvironment in solid tumors may limit the antitumor activity of TCR‐like CAR T cells. In this study, we observe an interesting phenomenon that the vast majority of target lesions located in lymph nodes showed different degrees of shrinkage after treatment, which may be closely related to the highly active immune microenvironment characterized in lymph nodes. Compared to the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment of solid tumors, the microenvironment in lymph nodes is enriched with a variety of immune effector cells, which can provide essential costimulatory signals and cytokines, supporting the activation of CAR T cells.

In this study, we observed notable differences in plasma protein expression levels among patients with varying treatment outcomes. KLK13, a member of the serine protease family, was first identified by Kapadia et al. 31 in 2003 and has been shown to be overexpressed in more than 50% of ovarian cancer tissues. White et al. 32 further confirmed this overexpression, reporting that KLK13 mRNA levels were significantly elevated in ovarian cancer. They suggested that KLK13 could serve as a potential biomarker for predicting ovarian cancer prognosis. In other tumor types, such as lung cancer, KLK13 has been associated with tumor cell migration and invasion through degradation of the extracellular matrix. In our cohort, KLK13 protein expression at baseline was lower in the SD_1 group. This downregulation may reflect tumor–immune interactions related to immunosurveillance, although the underlying mechanism remains to be clarified. In contrast, the role of KLK14, another member of the serine protease family, in ovarian cancer remains unclear. One study indicated that higher KLK14 mRNA levels were positively correlated with PFS in patients with advanced high‐grade serous ovarian cancer, 33 and Yousef et al. 34 similarly reported a negative correlation between KLK14 mRNA levels and serum CA125 levels. Taken together, these observations suggest that elevated KLK14 expression may be associated with a more favorable prognosis. Conversely, Zhang et al. 35 observed in vitro evidence suggesting that KLK14 may contribute to malignant behavior. In our study, we observed a significant upregulation of KLK14 expression in the SD_2 group. Given that KLK14 has been linked to extracellular matrix remodeling in prostate cancer, 36 we hypothesize that this upregulation may also be associated with the biological characteristics of ovarian cancer, potentially influencing tumor behavior.

CXCL17 is a chemokine derived from the airway epithelium, and its role in human cancers remains dual—potentially acting as either an antitumor or a protumor factor. 37 In this study, patients in the SD_2 group exhibited significant upregulation of CXCL17 at baseline. This elevation was associated with a potentially more immunologically active tumor microenvironment and increased immune‐cells infiltration. Previous studies have shown that upregulation of CXCL17 has a potential role in prompting immune cell migration, and in addition, it can promote immune cell chemotaxis when bound to its receptor CXCR8. Therefore, the upregulation of CXCL17 in this study may be associated with a tumor microenvironment permissive for immune‐cell recruitment and CAR T‐cell activity. However, given the limited number of evaluable cases (n = 9), these observations should be considered preliminary and hypothesis‐generating, requiring validation in larger cohorts.

In conclusion, KT127 targeting MSLN demonstrated a favorable safety profile and was well tolerated in patients with advanced recurrent or refractory ovarian cancer. The treatment was feasible and showed preliminary signs of disease stabilization. A mid‐trial amendment introduced nab‐paclitaxel into the lymphodepletion regimen, which may represent a potential confounding factor. Nab‐paclitaxel was included not as a cytotoxic agent but to transiently modulate the tumor stroma and improve CAR T‐cell trafficking. Taken together, these results support further clinical evaluation of TCR‐like CAR T‐cell therapy in larger studies to better define its therapeutic potential and to optimize future combination strategies.
